analysis.one_liner: Gives uninsured people discounted prescription drug prices through government-negotiated manufacturer rebates.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee on the day it was introduced and saw no hearing, no vote, and no further action before Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate rebate deals with prescription drug manufacturers, similar to the rebates drug companies already pay in Medicaid, and pass those savings to pharmacies that sell drugs at a discount to people who have no other prescription drug coverage. Drug makers that refused to sign rebate agreements would lose the federal tax deduction for their drug advertising and marketing expenses. The program could be shut down once the Affordable Care Act's health insurance exchanges were up and running.
analysis.who_benefits: People without any public or private prescription drug coverage — the uninsured and underinsured — would get drug prices discounted by rebates comparable to what Medicaid receives, purchased through participating pharmacies that would be reimbursed promptly and paid a dispensing fee.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a program in which HHS negotiates rebate agreements with drug manufacturers and requires that the rebates, on average, be comparable to the percentage rebate obtained under Medicaid, then passes the rebates to participating pharmacies as discounts for qualified residents. [S2] [S3]

Eligibility is limited to people not covered by any public or private program providing substantial prescription drug benefits, so the discount targets the uncovered gap rather than duplicating existing coverage, and applicants are screened for Medicaid and other programs first. [S2] [S3]

Participating pharmacies are guaranteed reasonable and timely reimbursement — no less promptly than Medicare pays — plus a dispensing fee, and may not be charged extra fees for joining the program. [S3]

Manufacturers that decline to sign rebate agreements would lose the federal income tax deduction for their drug advertising and marketing expenses, giving them a financial reason to participate. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Prescription drug manufacturers would pay quarterly rebates comparable in size to Medicaid's, and those refusing to participate would lose a tax deduction worth millions in advertising and marketing spending. Federal and state governments would cover administrative costs, funded out of the rebate money collected.

drawbacks.text: The program covers only people with no other drug coverage, so it would do nothing for people who have insurance but still face high copays or drug costs, and the Secretary could suspend or terminate the whole program once ACA exchanges were deemed operational. [S2] [S3]

Using the tax code to punish nonparticipating manufacturers' advertising expenses is a blunt enforcement tool that raises questions about whether HHS negotiation backed by that penalty could actually deliver rebates at the negotiated level, particularly for brand-name drugs with no competitors. [S3]

The bill leaves the discount amounts to later HHS rulemaking — a uniform average percentage method — so the actual savings for any individual purchaser would be uncertain at the time of enactment. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the uncovered population, the benefit is concrete: Medicaid-scale rebates passed through to pharmacies would cut the full sticker price this group currently pays, the group that faces the highest drug prices in the system. The costs fall on manufacturers, who would pay rebates they already pay for Medicaid and lose a marketing tax deduction if they opt out — a genuine penalty but one aimed at a concentrated, profitable industry. The main design weakness is that the program is explicitly temporary, tied to the ACA exchanges being declared operational, so the population it covers could lose the benefit without a replacement guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee on the day it was introduced and stayed there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote through the end of the Congress.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Michaud introduced the America Rx Act of 2011 on June 22, 2011, joined by Reps. Maurice Hinchey, Chellie Pingree, and Jesse Jackson Jr. as original cosponsors. [S3] [S4] [S5]
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to its Subcommittee on Health, where committee action ended. [S5]
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor consideration, and no further action appears before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Prescription drug manufacturers are better off: no rebates were negotiated for the uninsured and no manufacturer lost the advertising and marketing tax deduction. People without drug coverage continue to pay full retail prices. The bill had only four sponsors and no committee movement, so no legislator paid a price for its death.

for.name: Rep. Michael Michaud
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a government-negotiated rebate program for people without drug coverage.

for.name: Reps. Maurice Hinchey, Chellie Pingree, and Jesse Jackson Jr.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health Subcommittee and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors were House Democrats, and the bill died quietly in committee under a Republican House majority without any recorded vote showing where members stood.

industries.industry: Brand-name and generic prescription drug manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have required quarterly rebates comparable in average percentage to Medicaid's, and manufacturers refusing to join would lose the tax deduction for drug advertising and marketing expenses. The bill's death leaves this population paying full retail prices, the highest prices in the system.

Participating pharmacies would have been reimbursed promptly for the discounts they gave, paid a dispensing fee, and shielded from extra participation fees — new revenue with little added risk. Pharmacies lost that opportunity when the bill died.

The bill allows HHS and states to contract with pharmacy benefit managers and other third parties to run the program, creating a potential new government-contract role. The bill never advanced, so no contracts resulted.
